title: Computing the Internet Checksum
summary: Summarizes techniques and algorithms for efficiently computing the Internet checksum. It is not a standard but a collection of useful implementation tricks. It was updated by RFC 1141.

plainLanguage.summary: The Internet checksum is a calculation used by IP, UDP, and TCP to detect some data errors. RFC 1071 describes how to compute it efficiently on different processors, including ways to add several bytes at once and update the result when a field changes. The memo collects implementation techniques rather than defining a standard.

subtitle: A description of the Internet checksum and techniques for computing it efficiently.

tldr.problem: Computing the Internet checksum for every packet can consume significant processor time as other protocol processing becomes faster.
tldr.mechanism: The memo explains the 16-bit one's-complement sum and shows how to use word-sized operations, deferred carries, loop unrolling, combined copying, and incremental updates.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1071 is an Informational collection of implementation techniques, not a protocol standard. It was updated by RFC 1141.

today: RFC 1071 is Informational, not a standard, and was updated by RFC 1141. It collects checksum implementation techniques.

sections.title: How the Internet Checksum Works
sections.content:
The checksum used by IP, UDP, and TCP adds adjacent octets as 16-bit integers using one's-complement addition. To generate a checksum, the sender clears the checksum field, sums the relevant octets, and stores the complement of the result. For an odd number of octets, the last octet is paired with zero.

A receiver sums the same data including the checksum field. The check succeeds when the result is all one bits. On a two's-complement machine, any overflow from the high end is added back at the low end; this is called end-around carry.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender calculates a value from the packet and includes it with the data. The receiver repeats the calculation, including that value, and checks whether the result matches the checksum rule.

sections.title: Properties That Enable Faster Calculation
sections.content:
The checksum sum is commutative and associative when even and odd byte positions are handled consistently. This allows an implementation to add values in different groupings. A consistently byte-swapped calculation produces the same result with the result bytes swapped.

On a machine with wider words, an implementation can add several bytes at once and fold the result back into 16 bits. The memo also describes deferring carries, unrolling loops, and calculating the checksum while copying data so memory is read once.
sections.plainLanguage: The sum can be divided into groups and computed with wider machine words. That lets an implementation process more data in each step while preserving the checksum result.

sections.title: Incremental Updates and Examples
sections.content:
If a 16-bit header value changes, an implementation can update the checksum without summing the whole message again. Given the old value m, new value m', and old checksum C, the memo gives C' = C + (m' - m). A gateway changing an IP header's TTL is one example.

The memo works through hexadecimal examples calculated byte by byte, as 16-bit words, and as 32-bit words. It also shows how to combine two groups when the second group starts at an odd byte position.
sections.plainLanguage: When one header value changes, the checksum can be adjusted by the difference between its old and new values. The examples show that several calculation groupings produce the same result.

sections.title: Examples for Different Processors
sections.content:
The RFC gives core algorithm examples for C, Motorola 68020, Cray, and IBM 370 processors. The C example adds 16-bit words into a 32-bit accumulator, folds the sum to 16 bits, and complements it. The processor examples use techniques suited to their instruction sets.

The memo reports that the Motorola 68020 routine measured 134 microseconds per kilobyte with a 20 MHz clock. The IBM 3090 example measured 27 microseconds per kilobyte for data containing all one bits. These are measurements of the examples under the stated conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo shows how the same checksum can be implemented with different processor instructions. It reports example timings for two systems, rather than promising a speed for every implementation.

sections.title: The Reprinted Checksum Design Note
sections.content:
RFC 1071 includes Bill Plummer's 1978 IEN 45 note because it had not been widely available. The note describes properties that are useful in a checksum, including commutative and associative addition, efficient computation, unchanged message bytes, and incremental modification.

The note compares the Internet checksum with other approaches, including product codes and cyclic redundancy checks. It discusses trade-offs in computation, error detection, and whether intermediate gateways can still inspect packet fields.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix records an earlier discussion of why the checksum was designed as it was. It compares the checksum's useful properties with other error-detection approaches.

viz.caption: TECHNIQUES THE MEMO USES TO SPEED UP THE SUM

items.title: Use wider words
items.text: Add several octets in one machine operation, then fold the result.

items.title: Defer carries
items.text: Accumulate carries and fold them into the result later.

items.title: Update incrementally
items.text: Adjust the checksum when a field changes.
